wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_buttr.beta: Historically climbed as the 'direct route' up the Northeast Rib of the North Face — first done by David Harrah and Tom Miller in 1951. Modern parties climbing the fuller/harder version of the same buttress rate it Grade V, 5.8, AI2: a short approach leads to loose lower slabs, then thousands of feet of near-vertical vegetation (alder, turf, heather), a 5.5-5.8 rock band to a ~7,100 ft bivy, an exposed snow arête, and a short ice pitch to the summit ridge.

wa_colchuck_peak_east_ridge.beta: From Colchuck Lake, climb the Colchuck Glacier (axe and crampons; about 40-degree snow just below the col) to the col between Colchuck and Dragontail, which is the base of the ridge. Follow the ridge crest, negotiating Class 2-3 scrambling terrain. Several sections require hands but no protection needed. The granite is generally solid with good friction. Descent retraces the ascent.

wa_frying_pan_whitman_glaciers.overview: This is the standard glacier line up Little Tahoma, named for the two glaciers it crosses (Fryingpan and Whitman) rather than for the east-shoulder terrain feature; modern route guides describe "Fryingpan/Whitman Glaciers" and "East Shoulder" as the same standard route — same Summerland approach, same Whitman Notch crossing, same Class 3-4 summit block — first climbed August 29, 1894 by J.B. Flett and Henry H. Garrison. See the East Shoulder route entry on this peak for the closely related (likely identical) line.

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.notes: Note that this route and the Northwest Ridge route describe the same physical climbers' path up the west side of the mountain; the naming differs by source, the ground does not. Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,200-2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road, shared parking with the Barclay Lake day hike. Go around the outhouse and pick up the old overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — that is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail. Look for cairns and boot tread; this is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose. The tread is steep and often slick from the first steps, and there is no reliable water past the initial creek, so fill up at the car. After roughly a mile and 1,800 ft the path tops out on Baring's west ridge at about 4,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the basin and notch gully hold snow late
hazards: Steep, muddy, eroded unmaintained tread from the first steps
Cliffing out by holding the crest too long
Loose ash and obscured tread in the burn scar
Late snow in the basin and notch gully — axe and possibly crampons into mid-summer
Loose rock from the boulder field onward — helmet
No water above the trailhead creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The west ridge crest at about 4,000 ft is the handover point — the angle eases and the tread improves noticeably. Follow the crest generally east/southeast. Where the cliff bands appear, watch for the point where the path dips slightly below them into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge; staying too long on the crest is the recorded error and forces a downclimb back to the correct line. The 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope adds loose ash and hides the tread here.

The route then drops into a talus and boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully up to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit. That gully and basin hold snow late; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the vertical snow wall and its difficulty varies year to year. From the notch scramble up and right a short way, break onto an open slope, then trend left/north over class 2-3 boulder and heather to the base of the summit block, which is climbed on its left (west) side at class 3-4 to reach 6,127 ft.

wa_garfield_mountain_scramble.overview: Garfield Mountain is a rugged granodiorite massif of five named summits (Main/East Peak 5,519 ft, West Peak 4,896 ft, North Peak 5,101 ft, plus the Leaning Spire) rising more than 4,400 ft above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River in barely a mile — one of the steepest, most relief-dense peaks in the western Cascades. Despite a local reputation as a 'scramble,' every summit actually requires roped technical climbing: documented lines range from the 5.3 Southwest Ledges to the 23-pitch 5.10c sport route Infinite Bliss on the West Peak's south face, with the classic South Route (first ascended August 27, 1940 by Jim Crooks and Judson Nelson) involving sustained, loose Class 4 and low-5th-class terrain, extremely loose rock, and about eight rappels, six of them double-rope, on the way down.

wa_gunrunner.approach: Middle Peak shares the same approach as South Peak: from Downey Creek Trailhead, follow the southern Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route (Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake, Bachelor Creek) to reach the range's ridge. Middle Gunsight's east face is a known technical objective once on the ridge; expect a multi-day glaciated approach with route-finding and bushwhacking, not a drive-up or short-trail access.

wa_south_face_2001_variation.overview: Begins near the low-center of the south face at an obvious layback hand-crack (5.10, can be wet). Climb up and left to gain a rising ramp, then exit rightward in the upper section on fun 5.7-5.8 rock, topping out on the west ridge near the summit. Also cataloged as 'South Face Left', the FA is Mike Preiss & Don Preiss in 2004.

wa_mount_shuksan_sulphide_glacier.beta: From the campsites (6,245 ft for lower camps), head north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier up rolling steps. At approximately 7,600 feet, terrain flattens and route continues northeast toward summit pyramid. Standard route involves 3rd-4th class gullies to the summit, though the alternate Southeast Ridge is mostly 3rd/4th class with low-5th steps of about 5.3 when route-finding is selective; holding strictly to the crest adds two steps of 5.6 and 5.7 -- a roped climb, not a simple scramble finish.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the Shannon Ridge Trail's old roadbed to about 3,800 ft, then real trail onto the ridge crest to timberline near 4,600 ft, where snow often lingers into midsummer. Stay on the broad crest to the pass near 5,400 ft where the glacier and summit pyramid first appear; the camps sit on the glacier's edge at roughly 6,200 and 6,500 ft, with no reliable water late in the season.

Rope up at camp and climb north up the west side of the Sulphide Glacier over a series of rolling steps. Near 7,600 ft the angle eases; bear north-northeast across the flatter upper glacier to the foot of the summit pyramid around 8,400-8,500 ft. Large crevasses lie near high camp, bridges thin and blue ice appears as summer goes on, and old GPS tracks stop matching the open cracks late in the season.

The central gully up the south face of the pyramid, roughly 600 ft to the summit: start up the face just above the rock step at its base and trend slightly left. Early season it is steep snow; later it is blocky, stair-stepped rock that is solid for the Cascades but collects loose stones, and with parties above and below it becomes a rockfall chute. If the rock is iced, turn around. The descent comes back down this gully by rappel and downclimbing.

Instead of the gully, the ridge on its right (southeast) edge gives a roped alternative: a half-dozen or more short pitches, mostly 4th class with low-5th-class steps and big exposure. It suits a dry pyramid when the gully snow is rotten; plan to descend the central gully regardless, and carry a small rock rack and slings.

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.overview: North Twin Sister (6,644 ft) is the second-highest and northernmost summit of the Twin Sisters Range, a massif of dunite (mantle-derived, olivine-rich rock) about 10 miles southwest of Mount Baker. This line follows the mountain's standard west ridge on solid, high-friction olivine to the north summit - the same route as the separate West Ridge entry, described here as the unroped scramble most parties make.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.beta: There is no independently named 'Olivine Scramble' route; North Twin Sister has a single standard line — the class 3-4 west ridge on the mountain's famously grippy, orange-weathered dunite. This is the general scrambling description of that same route (the walk-up-oriented, unroped experience most parties actually have), while the separate 'West Ridge' route carries the more technical framing (mixed variation, roped sections). Expect sustained class 3 scrambling on exceptionally solid, high-friction rock, with short class 4 steps and multiple false summits near the top.

wa_south_early_winter_spire_east_buttres.beta: The specific route details are not well documented. This route designation appears in the database but is not clearly distinguished from the Direct East Buttress (5.11a, 9 pitch variant).

wa_the_chopping_block_south_route.beta: Climbers approach via Goodell Creek and Terror Creek to a high camp on the Stump Hollow ridge below the peak, then climb 3rd/4th class terrain with a short section of low-5th-class rock (5.4) to reach the summit. Because the Pickets guard several summits from a shared basin, parties frequently combine this peak with Mount Degenhardt, Mount Terror, or Inspiration Peak on the same trip. Note: the peak's standard lines are most often described as a 'Northwest Route' (Class 4, traversing ledges on the north face between the NE and NW ridges) and a distinct 'Northeast Ridge' (5.5, 4 pitches) — both broadly consistent in character and difficulty with the historic South Route described here, but the label 'South Route' is not attached to any specific established line, so treat route-specific pitch/rappel counts with caution.

pitch_detail.notes: High camp near Access Creek headwaters (~3,650-4,100 ft) up scree/talus and a dirt-filled gully to a col near 5,800-6,300 ft.
Heather, talus, and snowfield traverse across southeast-facing slopes to Luna Pass (~7,200 ft).
Broad ridge scramble from Luna Pass to the false summit.

~500 ft of loose, exposed ridge from the false summit to the true summit; one party reported a ~15 ft Class 4 chimney off the false summit followed by narrow ledges. Following east-side ledges avoids most Class 4 moves.
